summary: This RFC extends the Abuse Reporting Format and Sender Policy Framework so detailed reports of message authentication failures can be sent on demand. It also updates RFC 4408 by creating an IANA registry for SPF modifiers.

eli5.summary: When a mail check fails, the checker can mail a short report to the owner of the domain explaining what happened.

subtitle: Three new SPF record settings let a domain ask receivers to mail back reports when SPF checks fail.

tldr.problem: A domain that publishes an SPF record has no standard way to learn when mail claiming to be from it arrives by an unauthorized route.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds three optional SPF modifiers, ra= (where to send reports), rp= (what percentage of failures to report) and rr= (which kinds of failure to report), and the verifier mails Abuse Reporting Format reports to that address.
tldr.outcome: Domain owners can ask for failure reports on demand, and SPF modifier names now live in an IANA registry. The RFC updates RFC 4408 for that registry.

today: RFC 6652 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 4408 by adding the SPF modifier registry. Nothing in the unit metadata lists a later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Abuse Reporting Format (ARF) is a message format for sending reports of abuse in the messaging infrastructure, designed so that reports can be generated and consumed automatically. The Sender Policy Framework (SPF) is a path-based sender authentication mechanism: it checks the route a message took and produces a verified domain name that can then be evaluated, for example against a known-good list.

This RFC extends SPF with an optional reporting address and other parameters. The ARF extensions needed to carry these reports are covered in other documents, RFC 6591 and RFC 6650. The RFC also creates an IANA registry of SPF record modifiers to avoid name collisions.
sections.eli5: Mail checkers can already tell if a letter came by the wrong road. This RFC lets the checker tell the sender's owner about it.

sections.title: The ra, rp and rr Modifiers
sections.content:
A domain using SPF may want to know when messages arrive via unauthorized routing. The RFC defines three optional modifiers for SPF records.

  • ra= is the reporting address. It MUST be a local-part. The verifier builds the full address by appending @ and the SPF-checked domain, and SHOULD send a report there when mail claiming to be from the domain fails the SPF evaluation. An ra= found in a record reached through an include mechanism MUST be ignored.
  • rp= is the requested report percentage, an integer from 0 to 100 with a default of 100. It says what share of failures, chosen at random, should cause reports. The generator SHOULD NOT report more than that percentage, and MAY use the Incidents: field in ARF to say there were more incidents than reports.
  • rr= is a colon-separated list of tokens naming the conditions that should produce a report. The default is all.

If there is no ra= in the record, rp= and rr= MUST be ignored and the report generator MUST NOT issue a report.
sections.eli5: There are three little notes you can add to your mail rules. One says where to send reports, one says how many to send, and one says what kind of problems to tell you about.

sections.title: Choosing Which Failures to Report
sections.content:
The rr= tokens let the domain owner pick the circumstances of interest. Verifiers MUST NOT generate reports for incidents that do not match a requested report, and MUST ignore requests for reports not in the list.

The tokens map to SPF results: e covers "TempError" and "PermError", f covers "Fail", s covers "SoftFail", n covers "Neutral" and "None", and all asks for every report.
sections.eli5: You can say "only tell me about the serious problems" or "tell me about everything". The checker only sends what you asked for.

sections.title: The SPF Modifier Registry
sections.content:
IANA has created a Modifier Names registry under Sender Policy Framework Parameters, listing registered SPF modifier names and the documents that define them. New registrations follow the "Specification Required" policy and must give the modifier name, the defining document, and a status of Current, Deprecated or Historic.

The initial entries are exp and redirect (both from RFC 4408), plus ra, rp and rr from this document. This registry is how the RFC updates RFC 4408.
sections.eli5: There is now an official list of every extra setting an SPF record can use, so two people never pick the same name for different things.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Implementers are advised to read the security sections of SPF, ARF, RFC 6650 and RFC 6591. The RFC adds two points of its own.

Identity selection: a report must not itself fail SPF, or data loops could result. If the SMTP return address is not the null address, it MUST be chosen so it passes SPF MAIL FROM checks. If the report goes to a Message Submission Agent, the HELO/EHLO parameter SHOULD also be chosen to pass SPF HELO checks.

Report volume: the volume cannot be predicted, because the amount of abuse at receivers is unknown and can change quickly, so implementers ought to expect substantial volume.
sections.eli5: A report must not look fake to the very check it is reporting on, or the notes could bounce back and forth forever. Also, be ready for a lot of notes.

sections.title: Example Records
sections.content: The appendix gives three SPF records. The first is for a domain that sends no mail but wants reports. The second adds a reporting address to an existing record. The third sets a reporting address, a 10 percent sampling rate and a request for only error reports (rr=e).
sections.eli5: These are sample rule lines you can copy, from a simple one to one that asks for only a tenth of the reports and only certain kinds.
